angle: why Linear recreated Liquid Glass instead of adopting the system implementation
shareValue: A decision framework for knowing when a custom interface system earns its engineering cost.
problemStatement: Linear needed customizable mobile navigation, control over the material, and support extending beyond the newest system APIs.
solutionStatement: Linear recreated the parts of Liquid Glass that served its product while owning the navigation and material behavior.

source.title: A Linear spin on Liquid Glass

factChecks.claim: Linear says Apple’s APIs did not provide the control needed for its customizable navigation and that its custom approach could support users including those on iOS 18.
Linear says its iOS team had two engineers and describes recreating the material as the harder path.
Linear describes GPU-calculated moving light, variable edge blur, accessibility adaptations, and intentionally omitting refraction for readability.
A custom design system earns its cost only when system components prevent a product-critical behavior or experience.

slides.text: Recreate the useful principles—and own the behavior

slides.kicker: Linear says it could reduce readability in dense professional interfaces. Copying every effect would have weakened the product goal.

slides.kicker: Linear disclosed a two-engineer iOS team. Custom infrastructure also creates something the team must continue maintaining. The maintenance point is my analysis.

items: Can the team maintain it long-term?

captions.instagram:
Linear rebuilt Liquid Glass instead of taking the easier path.

The company’s real problem was not visual fashion. It needed mobile navigation that could adapt to different roles, expand beyond a conventional tab bar, and remain available beyond the newest system implementation. Linear says Apple’s APIs did not provide the control that product required.

Its solution was selective: recreate the material, model moving light on the GPU, add variable edge blur, preserve higher-contrast behavior—and omit refraction because it could hurt readability in a dense professional interface.

The trade-off is ownership. Linear disclosed a two-engineer iOS team and called this the harder path. My takeaway: build custom only when the missing behavior is product-critical and your team can maintain the result.

Which system component would you replace only if the product truly demanded it?
